pillar_reactions.evidence: Understood it and asked mechanical follow-ups rather than reacting emotionally: 'How do I decide if I want to do two trainings per week, three trainings per week, or five trainings per week?' Verbal response to the pillar itself was flat — 'Sounds good.' — and the rep had to prompt 'Anything specific about it that sounds good for you?'

The only pillar he volunteered a positive reaction to, and he tied it to his own life: 'Oh, I'm really glad that's the case, Richard, because I don't want to do any calorie counts. I don't want to be super hung up on what I eat and what time I eat. I just want to eat the right things... I just want to focus on my workout.'

Pushed back on the substance of the accountability pillar — when the rep asked whether he needed hard pushes, he said 'No, no, no. I don't think he needs to do that with me, honestly.' and argued his presence on the call was proof enough: 'the fact that I've spent the last 50 minutes talking about this, right? Shows... how serious I am.' Accountability was the pillar he valued least, which matters because it is the one being priced.

anchors.raw: the range I would be comfortable with is maybe $300, $400, maximum $500, but I don't think I will go up to $1,000 a month
anchors.note: He converted $6,000/6 months into $1,000/month within seconds of hearing it and priced it against a monthly personal-training rate. A $500/month ceiling against a $1,000/month effective rate is a 2x gap that no rebuttal on the call attempted to close.

anchors.raw: You told me it's like $300, $400 per month, and it's good. But $1,000, what are you offering?
anchors.note: His reference class is a certified gym trainer whose credentials are displayed — 'they show me his certificate, they show me his training, his background, his education, he's been verified'. That is the standard the offer was measured against and failed.

anchors.raw: I could very well spend $6,000 on a power rack, and work out for a year, or six months, and make that transformation myself
anchors.note: He has a specific competing use for exactly $6,000 — a garage power rack and cable system — that he has been weighing for a year or two. The offer was competing against a capital purchase, not against doing nothing.

anchors.raw: For $1,000, I would expect, well, we guarantee losing X amount of body fat. Well, we guarantee you, we're getting you to, you know, 75 kg in three months.
anchors.note: He named the specific thing that would have justified the price — an outcome guarantee — and the rep answered by putting the responsibility back on him ('you are the one that actually has to put in the work'). Worth noting against the Vik Singh call three days later, where a continuation guarantee was offered unprompted.

unmet_demand.want: Verifiable credentials and a track record for the coach — qualifications, named clients, institutional history
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Asked twice and never answered. The only proof offered was 'he's coached more than a thousand people' and Instagram before-and-afters, which he had already discounted: 'I don't know what kind of training they had, right? How many training sessions they had.'

unmet_demand.want: A results guarantee or a way to see value before committing $6,000
unmet_demand.why_unmet: No trial, no milestone-based refund and no outcome guarantee exists. The rep reframed the request as the prospect's responsibility rather than addressing it.

unmet_demand.want: A defined, structured payment plan he could evaluate
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The rep offered to 'split it up' but when asked 'Split it up how?' answered 'In the amount of payments that's needed' — no instalment count, no amount, no total. Nothing was actually put on the table to accept or reject.
